clinicalPearls: A common cause of chronic loose stools in an otherwise well, thriving pre-school child, typically between about one and five years of age
Stools are frequent and loose and may contain recognisable undigested food, giving the classic peas-and-carrots appearance
By definition the child grows well, is not dehydrated, and has no blood in the stool or systemic symptoms
It is often linked to dietary factors summarised as the four Fs: excessive fluid, fruit juice, low fat, and high fibre
It reflects rapid intestinal transit rather than malabsorption or infection
Diagnosis is clinical in a thriving child with a normal examination, and extensive investigation is unnecessary in the absence of red flags
Management is reassurance and dietary adjustment, normalising fluid intake, reducing fruit juice and sorbitol-containing drinks, ensuring adequate dietary fat, and avoiding excessive fibre
The condition is self-limiting and typically resolves by school age
reference.pathophysiology: Toddler's diarrhoea is a functional disorder of accelerated gastrointestinal transit rather than a disease of the gut mucosa. Excessive intake of fluids and of fructose- or sorbitol-containing drinks, together with a relatively low-fat diet, speeds transit and reduces the time available for water and nutrient reabsorption. The result is frequent loose stools containing undigested food residue, occurring in a child who is otherwise thriving with no evidence of malabsorption, inflammation, or infection.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic giardiasis or other gut infection
Carbohydrate malabsorption such as lactose intolerance or excess fructose or sorbitol intake
Inflammatory bowel disease in the older child
Cystic fibrosis or other pancreatic insufficiency when there is failure to thrive
additionalInvestigations: Careful growth monitoring and a detailed dietary history, which are the mainstay
Coeliac serology if there are any concerns about growth or symptoms
Stool microscopy, culture, and parasite testing if infection is suspected
Faecal elastase if pancreatic insufficiency is a concern
Full blood count and inflammatory markers if organic disease is suspected
Faecal calprotectin where inflammatory bowel disease is considered
Assessment of fluid and fruit-juice intake
redFlags: Blood or mucus in the stool
Nocturnal diarrhoea or systemic symptoms such as fever or vomiting
Onset in early infancy or persistence beyond the expected age
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent: this is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously, usually by around school age, without long-term consequences.
pitfalls: Subjecting a thriving child to unnecessary invasive investigation
Over-restricting the diet and causing nutritional harm, particularly inappropriate fat or calorie restriction
Missing coeliac disease or another organic cause when growth is faltering
Reflexly excluding milk without supporting evidence
Failing to address excessive fruit juice and sugary-drink intake
references: Rome diagnostic criteria for paediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders
management: Reassure parents that this is a benign, self-limiting functional disorder in a thriving child that requires no medication
Dietary modification targeting the four Fs: reduce excessive fluid and fruit-juice intake and cut fructose- and sorbitol-containing drinks
Normalise dietary fat and avoid an excessively low-fat, high-fibre toddler diet to slow intestinal transit
Maintain regular growth monitoring and plotting to confirm continued thriving
Avoid unnecessary investigation and restrictive elimination diets in the absence of red flags

Safety-net with review if faltering growth, blood in the stool, nocturnal symptoms, or systemic features emerge, prompting evaluation for organic disease such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease
